cls: Cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic blocker (single S-enantiomer of metoprolol)
quick: S-metoprolol ~25-100 mg once daily (ER); about half of racemic dose
Take with or after food, same time daily
Use only if clearly needed; monitor neonate
Small amounts in milk; usually compatible with monitoring
Heart rate, blood pressure, signs of heart failure
summary: S-metoprolol succinate is the single active S-enantiomer of metoprolol, marketed in some countries (e.g. India) as an extended-release cardioselective beta-1 blocker for hypertension, angina and stable heart failure. The S-enantiomer carries essentially all the beta-blocking activity, so effective doses are about half those of the racemic mixture (e.g. roughly 25-100 mg once daily ER). Clinical effects, cautions and interactions mirror metoprolol succinate. The single enantiomer is not separately FDA-approved; data derive from racemic metoprolol labelling and SmPC/regional sources.
indications: Stable, symptomatic chronic heart failure (with reduced ejection fraction) as add-on therapy
Reduction of cardiovascular mortality/hospitalisation in heart failure (class effect of metoprolol succinate)

dosage.d: S-metoprolol 25-100 mg once daily; titrate weekly to response
dosage.n: About half the corresponding racemic metoprolol dose
Titrate to symptom and heart-rate control

dosage.d: Start S-metoprolol ~12.5-25 mg once daily; double every ~2 weeks as tolerated
dosage.n: Target the highest tolerated dose; start low in NYHA III-IV

dosage.d: Start at a lower dose and titrate cautiously

admin: Swallow extended-release tablets whole or as scored halves; do not crush or chew
Take at the same time each day, with or after food
Do not stop abruptly - taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound tachycardia/angina
Check heart rate before dosing if bradycardia is a concern
Titrate gradually, especially when used for heart failure
moa: S-metoprolol is the pharmacologically active enantiomer of metoprolol and selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart. This reduces heart rate, myocardial contractility, cardiac output and renin release, lowering blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand. In heart failure, chronic beta-1 blockade attenuates harmful sympathetic activation and improves outcomes.

absolute: Severe bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, sick sinus syndrome (without pacemaker)
Cardiogenic shock or decompensated heart failure requiring inotropes
relative: Asthma / severe COPD (relative; cardioselective but use caution)
monitor: Signs of worsening heart failure during titration

preg: Beta-blockers cross the placenta and may cause fetal/neonatal bradycardia, hypoglycaemia and growth effects. Use only if clearly needed; monitor the neonate for bradycardia and hypoglycaemia.
lact: Metoprolol passes into breast milk in small amounts; it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding, but observe the infant for bradycardia and poor feeding.
renal: No major dose adjustment is required in renal impairment, as elimination is predominantly hepatic; use usual clinical caution.
hepatic: Metoprolol is extensively metabolised by the liver (CYP2D6). Reduce the dose and titrate cautiously in significant hepatic impairment due to increased exposure.

major: Verapamil/diltiazem (non-dihydropyridine CCBs) - severe bradycardia, AV block, hypotension
Other AV-nodal/bradycardic drugs (digoxin, amiodarone, clonidine) - additive bradycardia; do not stop clonidine abruptly with beta-blocker on board
moderate: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, quinidine, bupropion) - increased metoprolol levels
interactions.food: Take with or after food; food can slightly increase absorption of metoprolol.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it may enhance the blood-pressure-lowering effect.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers heart rate and blood pressure; may mask tachycardia of hypoglycaemia or hyperthyroidism.

serious: Worsening or precipitation of heart failure
emergency: Symptomatic severe bradycardia / complete heart block
Acute decompensated heart failure / pulmonary oedema

monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure regularly
Clinical signs of heart failure during dose titration
ECG if conduction abnormalities are suspected
counsel: Take it at the same time each day and do not stop suddenly - stopping abruptly can be dangerous
Swallow extended-release tablets whole (or as scored halves); do not crush
Report a very slow pulse, fainting, increasing breathlessness, ankle swelling or wheezing
Rise slowly to avoid dizziness; tell your doctor if you have asthma or diabetes
Limit alcohol while taking this medicine
pk: Beta-blockade within ~1-2 h; ER smooths the effect over 24 h
ER provides relatively flat levels; immediate-release peak ~1.5-2 h
Once-daily with the succinate extended-release formulation
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F), protected from moisture
pearls: S-enantiomer carries essentially all beta-1 blocking activity, so doses are about half the racemic metoprolol dose
Not separately FDA-approved; marketed in India/EU - clinical data extrapolated from racemic metoprolol succinate
Succinate (extended-release) is the formulation with heart-failure mortality benefit, unlike short-acting tartrate
Never stop abruptly - taper to avoid rebound hypertension, tachycardia or angina
Metabolised by CYP2D6 - poor metabolisers and CYP2D6 inhibitors raise exposure
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered the same day; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the usual once-daily schedule. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Overdose causes bradycardia, hypotension, heart failure, bronchospasm and possibly hypoglycaemia. Treat with supportive care, atropine for bradycardia, IV fluids/vasopressors, and glucagon for refractory beta-blocker toxicity; consider pacing.
